The current position features White's queen on f5 bearing down on the e5-pawn, which is undefended. Capturing it with the queen simultaneously creates an absolute pin on Black's knight along the diagonal leading to Black's king (the knight cannot move without exposing the king to check from the queen on e5). This also brings the queen to a square from which it attacks Black's undefended rook on g7.

Black's best reply is to relocate the rook to f7. This preserves protection of the now-pinned knight on c7 while keeping the rook active (it eyes the f2-pawn near White's king). Other squares either lose the rook for free (e.g., g6 is attacked by White's rook on c6 with no recapture available) or allow White to win the knight without compensation.

White follows up by capturing the pinned knight with the rook. Standard technique when piling up on a pinned piece is to capture first with the less-valuable unit (the rook). Black can recapture on c7, but White's queen on e5 will then recapture on c7, leaving White up a knight and a pawn overall. The pin prevents the knight from fleeing or assisting in defense, and no Black unit can safely capture the queen on e5. This line wins material by force while maintaining a strong attack.

The position features Black's advanced g2-pawn, which is one step from promotion and attacked by White's g6-rook along the open g-file. The key tactical idea is to promote immediately, creating an absolute pin on the g6-rook against the g7-king along the g-file. This is the "Pin" motif referenced in the puzzle.

- Black's first ply (g2g1q) advances the pawn with promotion to queen. The new queen on g1 directly attacks up the g-file, pinning White's rook (which cannot leave the file without exposing the king to check). The promotion square is defended by the f1-rook.
- White's only reasonable reply is to capture the new queen (g6g1), as ignoring it loses the queen for nothing. (Moving the pinned rook elsewhere along the file, such as to g3, allows the queen to capture it immediately.)
- Black's final ply (f1g1) recaptures the rook. Materially, this trades Black's promoting pawn for White's rook (net gain of a rook). The resulting rook on g1 also checks the king along the now-cleared g-file, as the capturing sequence has removed the blocking piece.

This line wins decisive material while maintaining the initiative; any deviation by White (e.g., not recapturing) allows Black to keep the queen for free. The sequence is forced and aligns with the puzzle's tactical theme, rating, and required ply depth.

The current position features Black's knight on f2 pinned against the king on f7 along the open f-file (f3-f6 are empty). White's key tactical move is to swing the rook onto the pinning line with Rh1-f1. This move has multiple purposes:
- It exploits the absolute pin on the knight (which cannot legally move off the f-file, as that would expose Black's king to check from the rook; all of the knight's possible moves are off-file).
- It saves the rook from the knight's attack on h1 while adding a second attacker against the knight (the white king on e2 is the other).
- The knight on f2 is undefended (no Black piece or pawn attacks f2), so it falls.

Black's best reply is to unpin by moving the king off the f-file (Kf7-g8). Other king escapes (e8 or e6) are similar but g8 keeps the king furthest from White's centralized pieces and bishops. Attempts to counterattack (e.g., Rc8-c2+) lose material even faster, as Bxd3 or similar captures are safe and undefended. Taking on d3 with the d8-rook also fails, as it allows Kxd3 (the pinned knight cannot recapture on d3).

White's follow-up (Rf1xf2) captures the pinned, undefended knight. This is preferable to Kxf2, as it keeps the king on e2 to continue defending the Bd3 (preventing Black from safely playing Rxd3 afterward). The result is a clean win of the knight with no compensation for Black, as recaptures on f2 are impossible and follow-up attempts to grab the Bd3 lose the d8-rook to Kxd3. This sequence is the principled tactical continuation based on the pin theme.
